newsitem.title: UK: UK rate rise bolsters evolving monetary framework.
newsitem.headline: UK rate rise bolsters evolving monetary framework.

text.p: Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke enhanced his reputation as a prudent manager of the British economy when he delivered a surprise quarter-point rate rise on Wednesday, just months before a general election.

But City economists said the Bank of England and country's fledgling monetary framework were the main victors having pushed inflation up the political agenda, forcing Clarke to raise the cost of borrowing to hit the tough 2.5 percent RPIX target.

"The Bank has come out of this very well. For the first time it looks like it is making a real contribution to domestic policy in run up to an election instead of being forced to shout from the sidelines," said Stewart.
Clarke and Governor of the Bank of England Eddie George fell out over the quarter-point rate cut in June, George arguing the economy was in no need of extra stimulation.
The subsequent run of data proved him right and on Wednesday Clarke was forced to reverse the cut, just four months later and well before its effects were fully felt in the economy.
Bank officials have played their cards very carefully, using the August inflation report to raise doubts that the government would hit its tough 2.5 percent inflation target.
It also upped the ante in the summer by stating that, internally, it was already discussing the merits of a pre-emptive rate rise.
After publicly losing the argument in May 1995, when its unheeded call for a half point rate rise was followed a by a run of weak economic data, the Bank can now claim an equaliser.
And economists said the rate rise has bolstered Britain's fledgling monetary framework.
Set up in early 1993 to help protect interest rates from political meddling, fears have grown in the City that it would fall apart as the election approached.
"The new policy framework is clearly acting as a constraint and Clarke is listening to the Governor's advise," said David Mackie, UK economist at JP Morgan.
Relations between Clarke and George may be more harmonious, at least for a while.
In the summer, sources close to the Bank said officials were growing frustrated with Clarke's dismissive attitude towards their advise.
"There was a feeling Clarke was being allowed to win the public relations battle without a fight," one source said at the time.
The Bank has a purely advisory role in setting interest rates, but Clarke has criticised it in recent month's, saying it is too gloomy in its inflation projections.
But with underlying inflation creeping up again -- it edged up to 2.9 percent in September after spending four months stuck at 2.8 percent -- Clarke may have to eat his words.
And City economists said the Chancellor has a long way to go before he goes down in history as the minister who put economics before politics and fortified Britain's tenuous inflation credentials.
The timing and size of the rate rise shows the Chancellor is still thinking in terms of politics, they said.

"It is pretty clear Clarke would have preferred to keep rates at 5.75 percent until the election, but he knew as the months went on the calls for higher rates from the Bank and other advisers would only get louder. It was astute to move early," said Stewart.

Above all, Clarke wanted to avoid raising rates at the next monetary meeting after the November budget on December 11 where a rate rise could be construed as an attempt to mitigate the effects of overly-generous tax cuts.
"But the real test will come next year," said Mackie.

George is unlikely to be satisfied with a paltry quarter-point rise. As the consumer-led recovery picks up pace later this year and next he is sure to seek another tightening, possibly as soon as January.
"The Governor is definately going to come back and ask for more in January and it will be then we see how Clarke responds to the pressure," said Mackie.

Kevin Gardiner, UK economist at Morgan Stanely agreed. "Since inflation risks remain it is likely George will come back for more. Clarke may not manage to get through to the election without another rise." -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7715
